title: The 4.3 That Wasn't Crossed Out
teaser: The budget allowed only RMB 1.5 million, yet all three projects were worth doing. Shen Qiao had already used shared weights to produce 4.3, 4.1, and 3.6. What changed the funding plan was not a new score, but the discovery that the evidence beneath those three numbers was not equally strong.
paragraphs: Before month-end, Shen Qiao had to lock the investment plan for the following year. The budget was only RMB 1.5 million. Project A, an automated packing line, needed RMB 900,000. Project B, a customer forecasting platform, needed RMB 800,000. Project C, a returns-grading program, needed RMB 600,000. All three addressed real problems. A could reduce labor and material waste. B might allow sales to see customer demand earlier. C could reduce rework while also responding to circularity requirements recently raised by two major customers. Equipment and software quotations expired at month-end, and finance could not leave all three decisions open.

To stop the meeting from turning into three departments proving that their own project mattered most, Shen Qiao asked everyone to confirm one set of criteria before seeing any project scores: financial contribution at 50 percent, strategic customer value at 30 percent, and implementation feasibility at 20 percent, with each category scored from one to five. Once all materials were submitted, A scored 4.1, B scored 4.3, and C scored 3.6. B ranked first, and B plus C required only RMB 1.4 million. Shen Qiao wrote 'B + C' in the corner of the page, and procurement began discussing the order in which the two contracts could be prepared.

During the finance review of B, someone stopped at a footnote. B had received a 5 for strategic customer value, and the most important support was the statement, 'Expected incremental revenue increases by 12%.' Tracing the number further showed that the 12 percent came from a supplier case in the consumer electronics industry. The company itself had interviewed only three priority customers. One was willing to share forecasting data continuously; the other two had said only that they were open to further discussion. Shen Qiao did not immediately challenge B. Instead, she asked all three projects to mark the source of evidence behind their key assumptions using the same questions. A's savings estimate came from ten months of internal labor and material records. C's rework estimate came from more than thirty thousand historical returns, but C also had one point that had not yet been tested: whether brand customers would actually cooperate with the new grading process.

The original weights and the scores of 4.1, 4.3, and 3.6 were locked. No one rescored anything. The team placed 'key assumption' and 'evidence source' beside the original table and ran one simple sensitivity case. If B's strategic customer value were 3 instead of 5, with all other weights and scores unchanged, its total would fall from 4.3 to 3.7, below A's 4.1. That did not prove B was wrong. It showed that the 0.2-point lead depended heavily on a judgment that the company's own customers had not yet validated. Shen Qiao drew a question mark beside 'B + C'. The 4.3 stayed exactly where it was.

The money was therefore not cut once from highest score to lowest. A's cost data and technical path were already supported by internal records, so it received RMB 900,000 for full implementation. C received RMB 300,000 first to launch with two customers and test whether they would cooperate with the new returns-grading process. B received RMB 100,000 for a data-integration trial, with a gate written down before any full purchase: within three months, at least four target customers had to provide forecasting data continuously. Finance wrote '900, 300, 100' on the sheet. RMB 200,000 remained uncommitted. All three projects were still being judged against the same strategic objectives; only the form of commitment differed according to what had and had not yet been demonstrated.

Three months later, A's savings were close to the original estimate. The two customers in C's pilot shortened returns-processing time by almost one day and agreed to continue using the new grading method. B had only two customers continuously providing forecasting data and did not reach the threshold of four. No one therefore wrote that the forecasting platform had 'failed,' and no one went back and erased its original 4.3. Before the next investment meeting began, Shen Qiao spread the old sheet on the table again and wrote two numbers beneath the evidence column in B's row: 2/4.
concept: Strategic project ranking is about handling multiple objectives under limited resources. Weights and scores can make trade-offs among financial contribution, strategic value, feasibility, and other criteria explicit and reproducible. But a total score should not hide differences in the evidence behind the estimates. When a high score depends heavily on an untested critical assumption, the evidence source and sensitivity of the result need to return to the decision separately. They can then shape whether the organization invests fully, stages the commitment, or validates the assumption first instead of compressing every uncertainty into one aggregate number.
explanation: All three projects have real value, and the weights are agreed before anyone sees the results, so the initial 4.3, 4.1, and 3.6 are not designed around a preferred project. The logical turn comes when B's 12 percent growth assumption is traced to a supplier case from another industry. Shen Qiao does not change the rules only for B. She asks A, B, and C to identify critical assumptions and evidence sources in the same way. The original scores remain untouched. A simple sensitivity case shows only that if one of B's key ratings falls from 5 to 3, its total moves from 4.3 to 3.7. The final choices—full investment in A, a limited pilot for C, and a four-customer evidence gate for B—show that scoring makes multi-objective trade-offs explicit while evidence strength shapes the form of commitment. The later 2/4 result tests the original critical assumption; it does not retrospectively prove that the 4.3 was 'calculated incorrectly.'
mapping: The three projects address cost, growth, and customer circularity requirements, while the budget cannot fund all of them → a genuine multi-objective choice under resource scarcity.
Before seeing the outcome, the team agrees on 50%/30%/20% weights and obtains A=4.1, B=4.3, and C=3.6 → scoring makes the trade-offs explicit and creates a reproducible initial ranking.

All three projects trace key assumptions using the same method: A has ten months of internal records, B's 12% estimate mainly comes from a cross-industry case, and C has strong historical data but still needs to test customer cooperation → evidence quality affects confidence in a score without letting management change the rules for one project.

The sensitivity case shows B can fall to 3.7; A receives RMB 900,000, C receives RMB 300,000 first, and B receives RMB 100,000 with a four-customer gate; after three months B reaches 2/4 → resource commitment is staged according to evidence strength while the original 4.3 remains visible.
boundary: Weighted scoring still has value, and imperfect evidence does not automatically mean a project should be delayed. The weights must fit the strategy, and decision makers should test whether results are sensitive to key weights or assumptions. Mandatory compliance, project dependencies, irreversible risks, and minimum resource thresholds may also take priority over the total score. Evidence quality is better shown separately than compressed into a new 'confidence score,' which would simply hide the differences again.
reflection: When two projects differ by only 0.2 points and one of the high scores depends mainly on an untested assumption, would you change the score or change the form of investment first?

calculation.budget: Total budget RMB 1.5 million; A requires RMB 900,000, B requires RMB 800,000, C requires RMB 600,000
calculation.weights: Financial contribution 50%; strategic customer value 30%; implementation feasibility 20%
calculation.initialCombination: B+C=RMB 1.4 million, within the RMB 1.5 million budget
calculation.sensitivity: If B's strategic customer value falls from 5 to 3, B's total score falls from 4.3 to 3.7
calculation.stagedCommitment: A receives RMB 900,000 directly; C receives RMB 300,000 first; B receives RMB 100,000 first; RMB 200,000 remains uncommitted
calculation.evidenceGate: B's gate is at least 4 customers continuously providing forecasting data; after three months the result is 2/4
